module_description: Module 6 covers non-API collection responsibly: HTTP scraping with requests/BeautifulSoup, headless browser automation, platform-specific scrapers, and the legal/ethical frame (platform Terms of Service, computer-access law, GDPR, UU PDP). Students practice rate limiting, polite crawling, and the distinction between public and permissible, plus reproducibility of scrapes.
core_concepts: Static vs dynamic pages; HTML parsing
Platform Terms of Service and computer-access law
Politeness, rate limiting, and reproducibility of scrapes
learning_outcomes: C3 Build a respectful scraper for a permitted public source
C4 Evaluate the legality and ethics of a scraping plan
C5 Document a scrape so it can be reproduced
methods_models: requests + parsers, Playwright/Selenium automation, yt-dlp for media, proxy/rotation concepts (used only in discussion)
Ethical checklist applied before any collection
evaluation_metrics: Reproducibility score of the collection (version, timestamp, hash) rather than model metrics
pitfalls_limitations: Scraping as a first resort; ignoring robots/ToS; breaking site stability; scraping personal data; treating scraped data as licensable
tools_stack: requests, BeautifulSoup, lxml, Playwright, yt-dlp, trafilatura, hashlib for checksums
commercial_platforms: Comparison of a permitted scrape vs API access for the same content; cost/benefit table
tools_access_cost: Some platforms block or legally challenge scraping; research-friendly routes vary. Verify current terms per platform and per jurisdiction before any collection
lab_activities: Scrape a permitted source (e.g. public news site or open directory), store with checksum and metadata
datasets_apis: Public news pages or open directories used as practice (not gated platform content)
assessment_methods: Written analysis/design document plus a short quiz; graded on correctness of concepts and quality of justification
data_collection_workflow: Define the question -> choose platform and access route -> collect via API or permitted scrape -> archive raw with checksums -> clean and document schema -> analyse -> preserve dataset and code
textbooks: Library guides on text and data mining for social media
Case-law summaries (e.g. hiQ v. LinkedIn) in data-law readers
key_papers: We Are Social / DataReportal 2026 report on platform data availability
trends_2024_2026: 2024-2026: anti-scraping engineering (dynamic rendering, signed requests) tightened, while open protocols reduced the need for scraping in some ecosystems
industry_relevance: Social media analyst, market-insights researcher, and data-journalist roles; this module is used for social listening, brand/issue monitoring, and audience research, and is referenced by industry certifications such as Meta Blueprint, Hootsuite Social Marketing, and Google Analytics.
localization_context: Taught with Indonesian-language material (IndoBERT/IndoRoBERTa/NusaBERT, InSet lexicon, Indonesian social datasets) so students can reproduce the analysis on local corpora; comparisons are made against Anglocentric benchmarks whose labels often transfer poorly.
ethics_regulation: Platform Terms of Service, UU PDP No. 27/2022 (Indonesian personal data protection), GDPR for EU-origin data, and IRB-style review for any data involving private individuals; public is not the same as consentable for social data.
case_study_scenarios: A client wants 2 million Instagram comments but has no API access. What are the legal/ethical options?
